questions.question: A genomics team runs a tightly coupled batch simulation that exchanges messages between nodes constantly and must finish in the shortest possible time. The nodes must be packed as close together as possible with up to 10 Gbps between instances. Which placement strategy should you choose?
options: Spread placement group across three Availability Zones
Cluster placement group with Enhanced Networking enabled
Partition placement group with seven partitions
Precision time placement group
questions.explanation: Cluster packs instances together in a single AZ and gives up to 10 Gbps between instances when Enhanced Networking is enabled, which is the recommended low-latency option. Spread is capped at 7 instances per AZ and isolates instances on separate hardware rather than packing them; Partition separates instances by rack set rather than packing them for bandwidth; Precision time addresses clock accuracy, not network throughput.
questions.keyTopic: Cluster: single AZ, 10 Gbps Enhanced Networking

questions.question: A compliance officer asks why you refuse to host a customer-facing multi-AZ application on a single cluster placement group, even though latency requirements are aggressive. What is the correct reason?
options: Cluster groups are limited to 7 instances per Availability Zone
A cluster group lives in one AZ, so an AZ failure fails every instance in it
Cluster groups cannot use instances larger than a medium size
A cluster group's instances cannot be reached over the internet
questions.explanation: The cluster strategy concentrates instances in a single Availability Zone, so an AZ failure takes down all of them at once — the documented downside of cluster. The 7-per-AZ limit belongs to spread groups; placement groups do not impose a size cap like medium instances; and reaching instances over the internet depends on networking, not the placement strategy.
questions.keyTopic: Cluster risk: AZ failure fails all instances

questions.question: An application has five critical EC2 instances that must each be isolated from the failure of the others, and the design should survive the loss of a single Availability Zone. The instances are spread across three AZs. Which strategy meets these requirements?
options: Cluster placement group in one Availability Zone
Spread placement group, with instances on distinct physical hardware
Partition placement group with one partition per AZ
Precision time placement group spanning the AZs
questions.explanation: Spread places each instance on different physical hardware, can span AZs, and is intended for critical instances that must be isolated from each other's failures. Cluster keeps everything in one AZ and fails together; Partition isolates groups of instances by rack set rather than per-instance and offers no per-instance isolation guarantee; Precision time is about clock accuracy, not failure isolation.

questions.question: A team needs to launch 10 instances per Availability Zone with per-instance failure isolation across two AZs, for 20 instances total. What is the outcome when they use a spread placement group?
options: It works, because spanning AZs removes the per-AZ instance cap
It works, because spread groups support hundreds of instances
It fails, because a spread group allows a maximum of 7 instances per AZ per group
It fails, because spread groups cannot span multiple Availability Zones
questions.explanation: The documented spread limit is 7 instances per group per AZ; spanning AZs does not raise that per-AZ cap, so 10 per AZ is not possible in a spread group. Options claiming the cap disappears or that spread reaches hundreds of instances misstate the limit, and the claim that spread cannot span AZs is the opposite of the source, which says spread can span AZs.

questions.question: A team runs Apache Cassandra on several hundred EC2 instances and needs the nodes to be aware of which rack-set segment they belong to so replication can avoid correlated failure. Which strategy fits and what limit applies per AZ?
options: Partition placement group, with up to 7 partitions per AZ
Spread placement group, with up to 7 instances per AZ
Cluster placement group, with 10 Gbps between instances
Precision time placement group, with PTP on Linux
questions.explanation: Partition groups scale to hundreds of instances, isolate instances by rack set across partitions, and are the documented fit for Cassandra/Kafka/HDFS-style workloads; the limit is up to 7 partitions per AZ. Spread caps out at 7 instances per AZ, far below hundreds; Cluster optimizes bandwidth within one AZ and offers no rack isolation; Precision time concerns accurate time sources, not rack isolation.
questions.keyTopic: Partition: up to 7 partitions per AZ

questions.question: How do instances in a partition placement group learn which partition they belong to, so a distributed application can be rack-aware?
options: They query an Amazon Route 53 private hosted zone for the partition ID
They read the partition information as EC2 instance metadata
They call a placement group API that returns the rack set name
They inspect the subnet ID, which is unique per partition
questions.explanation: The source states that EC2 instances in a partition group get access to partition information as instance metadata, which is what makes applications rack-aware. Route 53 hosted zones, a placement group API for rack sets, and per-partition subnet IDs are not how partition information is exposed to the instance.

questions.question: A data platform runs HDFS and Kafka across hundreds of EC2 instances and must limit the blast radius so that a hardware rack failure affects only the instances in that set, not the whole cluster. Which placement strategy should you select?
options: Cluster, so all instances share the lowest-latency network path
Spread, so every instance sits on distinct physical hardware
Partition, so instances are isolated into rack sets that fail independently
Precision time, so event ordering is preserved during the failure
questions.explanation: Partition spreads instances across partitions backed by different rack sets, so a partition failure can affect many instances in that partition but not the other partitions — exactly the requested blast-radius limit, with HDFS/Kafka as documented use cases. Cluster concentrates everything and fails together; Spread is capped at 7 instances per AZ and cannot host hundreds; Precision time is about clock accuracy, not failure domains.
questions.keyTopic: Partition: hundreds of instances, rack isolation

questions.question: A trading firm must record the order in which financial events occur and needs the most accurate time source available on its EC2 instances, including hardware timestamping. Which choice matches the source?
options: Precision time placement group using enhanced Amazon Time Sync and a PTP hardware clock on Linux
Precision time placement group using standard NTP and a PTP hardware clock on Windows
Cluster placement group using Enhanced Networking for tighter timestamp correlation
Spread placement group across AZs with Amazon Time Sync on each instance
questions.explanation: Precision time groups give direct access to high-precision time sources: enhanced Amazon Time Sync Service (more accurate than standard NTP) plus a PTP hardware clock with hardware packet timestamping, which is Linux only. Standard NTP plus Windows fails both the accuracy and the Linux-only constraint; Cluster solves bandwidth, not clock accuracy; and Spread does not provide the enhanced time sources or PTP clock.
questions.keyTopic: Precision time: Amazon Time Sync, PTP clock (Linux)

questions.question: A workload needs accurate timestamps and event ordering for financial records, but the network throughput requirement is modest. Why is the precision time strategy the right answer rather than cluster?
options: Because precision time gives 10 Gbps between instances and cluster does not
Because precision time addresses clock accuracy and timestamping, while cluster optimizes latency and bandwidth
Because precision time spans multiple Regions, while cluster is regional
Because precision time removes the 7-instance-per-AZ limit
questions.explanation: Precision time is a placement choice about access to high-precision time sources and PTP hardware timestamping, which is what financial timestamping and event ordering require. The 10 Gbps figure is the cluster benefit, not precision time's; neither strategy is described as spanning multiple Regions; and the 7-per-AZ cap is a spread limit that precision time does not address.
questions.keyTopic: Precision time use cases: financial timestamping
